name: Emeka Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven o'clock I'm at Fairbank. First job is feeding the suckler cows, that's beef cows with their calves at foot, about ninety head in winter. Then fences, gates, water troughs, whatever's broken. In summer it's the wheat, and I drive the grain trailer at harvest. I'm not a natural farmer. I can't tell a sick calf from a sulky one yet, Mr Okafor has to tell me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before Fairbank?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-one years a lorry mechanic at Banks Garage on the ring road. The old man retired, sold the place, and now it's flats. Mechanic jobs round here want you plugging a laptop into the engine, and that's not me, so I went where the work was. The money's poor, less than the garage paid, and Ana cleans at the school at six every morning so we can keep the lights on. Only good thing is Mr Okafor's old Massey tractor. When it coughs, I'm the one who knows why.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI or computer tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've got a phone that makes calls and sends texts. My daughter keeps trying to put things on it. I tell her I fixed lorries for thirty years with a spanner and my ears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd guess anyway. Lots of talk, then everybody goes back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly. I don't argue about it. At the pub I'd say the same thing I say about electric lorries: let's see it work in February in the mud first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job, more or less. I'm not worried about a computer that answers emails. I'm worried about the new tractors that drive themselves, and if this is the hype version, they stay expensive and Okafor keeps his old Massey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, feed the cows, fix what's broken. Maybe ask Okafor to show me more of the stock work, the calving and that, so I'm not just the fence man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. That's what I'd expect. Nothing to get worked up about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the old Massey keeps you useful. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new ones you can't fix in a field. The computer says fault code, you ring the dealer, the dealer comes Tuesday. The Massey I can strip and fix with what's in the back of my van. As long as Okafor keeps old kit, I'm worth something to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the work right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cold. And being the slow one at 58. Last spring a heifer was calving wrong and I stood there useless while Okafor's nephew, he's 24, sorted it. You don't forget that.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, quietly, and that I'd want to see these things work in February in the mud first. I don't argue about it.
S0.think: It means I keep my job. I'm not worried about computers answering emails, I'm worried about self-driving tractors, and in this picture they stay too expensive.
S0.do: Keeps turning up, feeding cattle and fixing what's broken. Asks the farmer to teach him more stock work like calving so he's not only the fence man.
S0.feel: Fine, nothing to get worked up about.
S0.quote: As long as Okafor keeps old kit, I'm worth something to him.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka's worth on the farm rests on keeping an old tractor running, and he knows it. He has no interest in AI tools and dismisses them with a mechanic's pride. Being shown up by a 24-year-old during a calving still stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I believe. That's how it went with the lorries. One by one the jobs went over to the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd keep my mouth shut, mostly. If Okafor asked, I'd say buy what makes sense, but keep someone who can fix it. I wouldn't say anything online, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's the garage again. When the trucks went electronic, the young lads with laptops got the work and I got the old ones. Same here: once Okafor gets a new tractor with all the kit, my one trick is gone, and I'm a slow farmhand with bad knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what Okafor buys. If a new tractor turned up, I'd start putting money away, even 10 a week, and cut the beer and the betting on the horses on a Saturday. I'm not going on a course. I'm 58, I'd rather spend it on the job I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like hearing a knock in an engine you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go on a course. What if Okafor paid for one on the new tractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he paid and it was on work time, I'd go. I'm not stupid. But I'd be honest with you, I'd struggle. I tried the diagnostic laptop at the garage once and it was like reading a menu in a language I don't speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. She worries enough. I'd tell her when it actually happened, not before. No sense two of us lying awake over a tractor that might not come.

S1.say: I'd keep quiet at work, and if asked I'd tell the farmer to buy what makes sense but keep someone who can fix it. I'm not online.
S1.think: It's the garage again: once the farm gets a new computerised tractor, my one useful skill is gone and I'm a slow farmhand with bad knees.
S1.do: Watches what the farmer buys and starts saving 10 a week if a new tractor arrives. Cuts beer and Saturday betting, and would go on a course only if the farmer paid and it was on work time.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest, like hearing a knock in an engine he can't place.
S1.quote: Tight in the chest. Like hearing a knock in an engine you can't place.
S1.fieldNote: Emeka sees slow change as a replay of his garage, where electronics pushed him onto the old lorries. He said no to courses, then agreed if paid and on work time, while expecting to struggle. He would keep his worries from his wife until something actually happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. Then I'm finished at 60. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say government had better have a plan, because they'll have half the country out of work. I'm not one for marches, but I'd vote for whoever had a real plan, left or right, I don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out at Fairbank as soon as the robots worked. Okafor's a decent man but he's not a charity, he's got margins like everyone. And there's nothing else here. The scrapyard, the feed mill, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything. The van goes, I'd use Ana's car. The TV package, the betting, the beer, all gone. I'd go to the scrapyard and ask about work, breaking old machines for parts, because that'll be busy. And once I was laid off, I'd ask my son for help, and I'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like when Banks Garage closed, but there's no next place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to the scrapyard. Why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if every farm is buying robots, every old tractor and trailer goes for scrap or parts. Somebody's got to take them apart. It's dirty work, but I know how a machine comes apart better than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change things, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't get to the pension, can't save, can't learn anything new, not at my speed. Ten years, I'd be 68, I'd shrug. Two years, I'm a 60-year-old man asking his son for money.

S2.say: I'd say government had better have a plan, because half the country would be out of work. I'd vote for whoever had a real plan, left or right.
S2.think: I'd be out of the farm as soon as the robots worked, because the farmer has margins like everyone. There's nothing else here but the scrapyard and the feed mill.
S2.do: Sells his van and cuts TV, betting and beer. Asks the scrapyard about work breaking up old farm machines, and asks his son for help once laid off.
S2.feel: Sick, like when his garage closed but with no next place to go.
S2.quote: Two years, I'm a 60-year-old man asking his son for money.
S2.fieldNote: Emeka is not political but would vote for whoever had a plan. His one practical idea, breaking old machines for scrap, is clever and grounded in his skills. Asking his son for money is the outcome he dreads most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. Close to the line, not over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: government needs a plan, and five years is enough to make one. At work I'd tell Okafor's nephew to learn the robots, because he's young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's three years short of the pension, and three years is something you can maybe scrape through with the scrapyard and a bit of work here and there. It's tight but it's not the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Fairbank as long as possible and put everything spare into savings, even if it's only 15 a week. I'd talk to the scrapyard early, get my name in. I'd look into taking my pension early, if they let you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not sick. Worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The neighbours. When Harlow's farm across the road gets one of those robot tractors and it works through a wet winter, then I'd know. Until then it's just talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for marches. Would anything change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they cut the pension age again, I'd go. That's the one thing. You work forty-odd years for it, they can't move the line when you're nearly there.

S3.say: I'd say government has five years to make a plan, so it should. I'd tell the farmer's young nephew to learn the robots.
S3.think: Five years puts me three years short of my pension, which I might scrape through with scrapyard work and odd jobs. It's tight but not the end.
S3.do: Keeps working at the farm and saves 15 a week. Gets his name down at the scrapyard early and looks into taking his pension early.
S3.quote: When Harlow's farm across the road gets one of those robot tractors and it works through a wet winter, then I'd know.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Emeka's fear became manageable arithmetic: three years to bridge. His test for the technology is practical and local, a neighbour's tractor surviving a wet winter. The only thing that would get him to protest is a change to the pension age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68. I'd be in my shed by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not my problem, honestly, and I'd say it with a laugh. It's the young lads who'll have to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm safe, as far as these things go. I'd get my pension at 66, and we've lived on little before. I'd worry for my grandson, he's 8, but that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Keep working, keep my head down, fix the Massey. Maybe tell my daughter to be careful about what her boy studies, later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Quite relaxed, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'as far as these things go'. What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, mainly. If they go before 66, that's the real problem, not robots. And if Okafor sells up, there's no Fairbank to work at at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fix old engines for people in the village, for cash or for a bottle. Lawnmowers, motorbikes, whatever. I'd like that. No one's building a robot to fix a 1990s lawnmower.

S4.say: I'd say with a laugh that it's not my problem, and the young ones will have to sort it out.
S4.think: I'm safe as far as these things go, because I'd get my pension at 66 and we've lived on little before. My grandson is the one I'd worry about later.
S4.do: Keeps working and keeps his head down, maintaining the old tractor. Plans to fix old engines for neighbours in retirement, and may advise his daughter on her son's studies later.
S4.quote: No one's building a robot to fix a 1990s lawnmower.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts Emeka past his pension, and he relaxed completely. His real risks are his knees and the farmer selling up, not robots. He lit up describing a retirement fixing old engines for cash.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything else I can see a way through, slow and ugly, but a way. What would help is being able to take the pension early without it being cut to nothing, and a bit of money for older workers who get laid off, so you're not begging your kids.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old machines. Everyone talks about robots, nobody asks what happens to all the old tractors and the men who know them. There's a lot of us.

headlineQuote: I fixed lorries for thirty years with a spanner and my ears.
portrait: Emeka Diaz is 58 and spent thirty-one years as a lorry mechanic until his garage was sold for flats; for four years he's been a general hand at Fairbank, a beef and wheat farm. He's slow with the stock work but keeps the farmer's old tractor running, which he sees as his only real value. He's pragmatic, not political, never uses AI and keeps his worries from his wife Ana, who cleans at a school. Slow change reminds him of the garage, and fast AGI would leave him at 60 asking his son for money. With ten years he relaxed completely and talked about fixing lawnmowers in retirement.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would leave him out of work at 60 with no savings and no way to reach his pension.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to take his pension early without a big cut, and some money for older workers who are laid off so they don't have to rely on their children.
